newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-LIONS FOLLOW ILLUSTRIOUS FOREBEARS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-LIONS FOLLOW ILLUSTRIOUS FOREBEARS.

text.p: Choosing the greatest British Lions' side from the ages, an occasional source of saloon bar debate, could be drastically simplified.
Select the 1955 Lions' backs, place them behind the 1974 forwards and a XV emerges who could have taken on any team in the history of rugby union.
Ian McGeechan, coach of the latest Lions' team who meet world champions South Africa in the first of a three-test series on Saturday, has one eye on the history books.

Already he has gone a long way to restoring the credibility of British and Irish rugby by inspiring some team and individual performances which seem scarcely credible after an eminently forgettable Five Nations' championship.
But only the test series will reveal if the 1997 Lions can reach the same stature as the 1955 and 1974 teams, who wore the famous red strip with such distinction throughout South Africa.

In 1955, Tony O'Reilly, Jeff Butterfield and Cliff Morgan dazzled opponents and spectators alike in a drawn series. Danie Craven, world rugby's greatest if most controversial figure, called them the best side ever to visit the republic.
Nineteen years later a Lions' side led by the formidable Ulsterman Willie-John McBride went one better, winning the test series and going unbeaten through the hardest tour of them all.

McBride locked the scrum with Scotland's Gordon Brown behind an uncompromising front row of Ian McLauchlan, Bobby Windsor and Fran Cotton. Loose forwards Roger Uttley, Mervyn Davies and Fergus Slattery completed an awesome pack.
The 1955 Lions had a fine pack based on a core of rugged Welshmen with hooker Bryn Meredith at their heart.
In 1974 the backline contained the incomparable J.P.R. Williams at full-back, Welshmen Gareth Edwards and Phil Bennett at half-back and McGeechan himself as one of the centres.
But essentially the 1955 successes came through the backs; those of 1974 through the forwards.
South Africa, a land without television and dependent for its news of the outside world on print and radio, had never witnessed anything like the 1955 Lions' backs.

The red-haired O'Reilly had speed to burn on the wing, as well as strength and vision. He scored 16 tries in 1955 and 22 in Australia and New Zealand four years later. A man of wit and intelligence, he is now one of Ireland's richest businessmen.
England's Butterfield was fast, clever and stylish at centre while Morgan, a product of the Rhondda valley, was one of the great Welsh fly-halves.
Morgan, small and dark with magic in his feet, relished the hard grounds of South Africa.

He scored one of the supreme individual tries in one of the most exciting of all tests when the Lions defeated the Springboks 23-22 in the first test before a world record crowd of 95,000 at Ellis Park.

The Lions, playing with 14 men in the second half in an era before replacements were allowed, led 23-11 before tiring. South Africa scored in injury time but the simple conversion which would have won the match went wide.
O'Reilly, who along with Butterfield had scored a try for the Lions', refused to watch the final kick.
"I was," he said later, "in direct communication with the Vatican."
The 1955 side won both their tests on the fast grounds of the high veldt but lost the other two on the softer pitches at sea level.
McBride's side were equal to any conditions and to any occasion.

A number of key players, including McBride, had been members of the 1971 side who won a series in New Zealand for the first time and the status of British rugby in those days has not been matched since.
McBride had learned about South African rugby the hard way, playing on losing Lions' sides in 1962 and again in 1968.
Determined this time not to bow to physical intimidation, McBride instituted the controversial "99" call when he felt the opposition were over-stepping the mark.
At the call, each of the Lions would pitch into the opposition on the theory that any local referee, however inclined toward the home side, could not send an entire team off the field.

The tactics were crude, illegal but ultimately effective. The Lions were unbeaten on tour, won the test series 3-0 and were denied victory in the 13-13 fourth test draw when the South African referee disallowed an apparent try by Slattery in the final minute.

Twenty-three years on, neutral referees are the norm. Television cameras at every angle capture any transgressions and the professional game of the 1990s is certainly cleaner than the amateur version of the 1950s and 1970s.

What has not changed is the ultimate physical challenge of taking on the Springboks in South Africa. Success for the 1997 Lions would ensure a place for them and their visionary coach alongside the 1955 and 1974 heroes.
